items.text: The `download_apps.update_api_key` column already exists in the schema but is unused. It was originally provisioned for external update notifications. The new webhook_subscriptions table supersedes its purpose — it can be left in place or cleaned up separately.

items.context: Webhooks can be scoped at different levels. Bundle-wide subscriptions fire for all apps in a bundle. App-specific subscriptions fire only for that app. This affects the data model (nullable app_key column) and matching logic.

options.label: Both bundle-wide and app-specific
options.rationale: Maximum flexibility. A nullable app_key column means bundle-wide if NULL, app-specific if set. Matching query: WHERE bundle_key = $1 AND (app_key IS NULL OR app_key = $2). Slightly more complex but covers all use cases.

options.label: App-specific only
options.rationale: Simpler model — every subscription targets one app. Consumers that want all events must create one subscription per app. Less flexible but simpler matching.

items.context: After UpsertAsset succeeds, the webhook needs to be dispatched. The delivery model affects response latency, reliability, and complexity. For V1 we want simplicity since there's no message queue infrastructure.

options.label: Fire-and-forget goroutine per delivery
options.rationale: Simplest approach. Spawn a goroutine with a 10s HTTP timeout. Handler returns immediately. Failures are logged but not retried. Good enough for V1 — consumers can poll as fallback.

options.label: Synchronous delivery before response
options.rationale: Handler waits for webhook delivery before responding. Simpler to reason about but adds latency to publish operations. Not recommended for production.

options.label: Background worker with in-memory queue
options.rationale: A channel-based worker pool processes deliveries. More controlled concurrency but adds complexity. Worth considering if volume is expected to be high.

items.context: The webhook POST body needs to contain enough information for consumers to act on publish events without making follow-up API calls. Too little data forces polling; too much data couples consumers to LPBS internals.

options.label: Event envelope with asset summary
options.rationale: Include event type, timestamp, and key asset fields: bundle_key, app_key, platform, release_version, artifact_id, artifact_source. Enough for consumers to identify what changed and fetch details if needed.

options.label: Full asset + artifact objects
options.rationale: Include the complete DownloadAsset and DownloadArtifact JSON. Consumers have all data immediately but payloads are large and tightly coupled to internal types.

options.label: Minimal notification (event type + IDs only)
options.rationale: Just event type, bundle_key, app_key, and artifact_id. Very stable contract but forces consumers to make a follow-up GET call for details.

items.context: Webhook consumers need to verify that payloads came from LPBS. HMAC-SHA256 signing is standard practice. The question is how secrets are managed — auto-generated vs user-provided, and whether they're readable after creation.

options.label: Auto-generate on creation, write-only
options.rationale: LPBS generates a crypto-random secret when a subscription is created. Secret is returned once in the create response, then never shown again in list/get. Most secure — prevents accidental leakage via API browsing.

options.label: User-provided secret, write-only
options.rationale: Admin provides the secret at creation time. Allows shared-secret patterns where both sides already know the key. Still write-only in list/get.

options.label: Auto-generate, always readable
options.rationale: Secret is visible in all API responses. Simpler for debugging but higher leakage risk.

plan_updates: Created initial plan.md with all 13 mandatory sections. Phases 1-5 outline data model, service, integration, admin endpoints, and tests. Problem clarity is high from codebase exploration. Key decisions on granularity, delivery model, payload schema, and secret handling are pending user input.
